Elon Musk: Tesla’s Robotaxi Goal Is Speed — But Safety Comes First

With Robotaxi, our goals are very ambitious, but we do need to be cautious about causing any accidents or causing any harm to anyone.

Although there are, I think, 30 to 40,000 automotive deaths per year in the United States alone, most of those do not generate any publicity.

You never really read about almost any of those.

But if we injure even one person, it becomes a worldwide headline news story, and regulators will immediately clamp down on all our activities.

And we don't want anyone to get hurt.

So, we are scaling Robotaxi as fast as humanly possible, but while making sure that we do not harm anyone at all.

Ideally, we don't even want to run over a pet.

So, that's really the constraint: we want to go as fast as possible, but without causing harm to anyone.

Elon Musk: “Optimus Will Be The Biggest Product Ever Created”

Let's see Optimus. You know, as you've heard me say before, I think Optimus will be the biggest product ever. But it is a very complex problem to solve. It's one of the hardest things to solve.

To make a humanoid robot that can do tasks that you simply ask it to do, or show it a video, and it can do the task without any programming — like, no one's ever achieved this.

And there are many challenges in the electromechanical design of the robot, to achieve sufficient dexterity and reliable hands, to be very reliable and have long, long wear and tear.

But, I mean, it's good to be out in the field and not break down. Otherwise, you get this 70-kilogram robot that just flopped over, and you could carry it around like a baby, you know.

And we don't want Optimus to go haywire.

So, it's a lot of work to scale, to get the design right, and to scale production.

And I really want to emphasize here that the production scaling challenge is very, very substantial.

So this is going to be the hardest product to scale manufacturing that we've ever made at Tesla, because everything on the robot is new.

And the difficulty of scaling the production up is proportionate to the newness of the parts in the robot.

Most people focus on Starship’s height and thrust.

The number that actually matters is cost per kilogram to orbit.

Falcon 9 already cut it from the Shuttle era’s ~$54,500/kg down to around $1,500/kg. Starship is targeting under $100/kg.

That’s a 500x reduction in roughly 25 years.
That single metric is what makes Mars, lunar bases, and large-scale orbital industry possible. 

Everything else is a consequence of driving launch costs down.

Reusable rockets aren’t just cool engineering — they’re the fundamental economic unlock for becoming multiplanetary.

The signal has never been more bullish on $TSLA 

Tesla just dropped Q2 2026 results: revenue crushed at $28.2B (up 26% YoY, big beat), deliveries strong at 480k+, energy storage at record 13.5 GWh, and services exploding +50%. EPS missed and free cash flow went negative — exactly as expected when you’re pouring >$25B in CapEx into the actual future.

But look at what’s actually happening under the hood:

•  Cybercab production has started at Giga Texas. Employee rides already running.
•  Robotaxi is live in 7 major metros, unsupervised expanding, with more coming.
•  Optimus lines are being installed right now at Fremont (on the old S/X footprint). Production planned this year. First units going into the Optimus Academy for training data.
•  FSD attach rate in North America >55% of new deliveries. Record net new subscriptions. v14 lite rolling out.
•  AI training compute in Texas more than doubled in H1. Cortex 2 ramping. Semiconductor fab progressing.

Tesla’s own words in the shareholder update:

“We’ve never been more optimistic about the future.”

This is the classic Amazon 2016 / early Tesla moment. The market is staring at near-term margin pressure and calling it a miss. Meanwhile Tesla is converting factories, building the robotaxi fleet, and standing up humanoid production at scale. The current auto + energy business is funding the next three acts of the company.

When the biggest real-world AI company on Earth is simultaneously:

1.  Ramping purpose-built autonomy hardware
2.  Scaling unsupervised robotaxi miles
3.  Installing humanoid production lines
4.  Doubling AI compute
…while demand is recovering and FSD adoption is accelerating — that is not a mixed quarter. That is the clearest long-term signal we’ve ever seen.

The short-term noise is the cost of building the future. The signal has never been cleaner or more bullish.
